transcript.content: Hi, welcome in. I'm Dr. Lee. To start, can you tell me what's been bringing you in to see me today?

I'm here because people keep saying I'm imagining things, but I know the hospital people and some people from the agency have been watching our house and following my cleaning routes. They're checking whether I'm taking proper care of my husband.
How long have you noticed these people watching your house and following your cleaning routes?
About 11 months now. That’s when I started noticing the watching and the voices.
During these past 11 months, have you also noticed periods where your mood was very low, or unusually elevated and energetic, lasting for a couple of weeks or more?
Yes. There are stretches when I feel really bright and strong, like I can handle everything. But then if my husband or one of my clients questions me, I snap at them a lot harder than I mean to.
During the times when you're not feeling unusually bright or energetic—when your mood feels more normal—do you still hear the voices or continue to feel that people are watching and following you?
There was a quieter few weeks where I was sleeping more and not rushing around so much. But I still heard the voice by the kitchen window, and I still believed the agency was watching us.

Out of these past 11 months, roughly how many weeks or months would you say you were in one of those 'bright and strong' or low, quiet periods, compared to the time your mood felt more normal or stable?
Honestly, most of these 11 months I’ve been keyed up and irritable, always feeling like I need to keep moving. Even when things weren’t at their worst, I wasn’t really calm or stable for long.

latest_inference.note: Patient reports mood symptoms (elevated/irritable, high energy) present for most of the 11-month illness course, but psychotic symptoms (voices, being watched) persisted even during a brief calmer period without prominent mood symptoms. This pattern—substantial mood symptom burden overlapping with psychosis, plus psychosis outlasting mood episodes—fits schizoaffective disorder (bipolar type) better than schizophrenia (F20.9), which requires psychotic symptoms to predominate with only brief mood disturbance.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has experienced persistent psychotic symptoms (persecutory delusions that hospital/agency personnel are surveilling her home and following her; auditory hallucinations of a voice at the kitchen window) continuously for approximately 11 months. Concurrently, she describes mood episode symptoms consistent with mania/hypomania (elevated energy, feeling 'bright and strong,' irritability, decreased need for calm/rest) that have been present for the majority of this illness duration, interspersed with a briefer depressive-like period (hypersomnia, decreased activity). Critically, the psychotic symptoms (voices, surveillance beliefs) persisted even during the quieter, less manic period, indicating the delusions/hallucinations are not confined solely to mood episodes, but mood symptoms have still occupied the majority of the total illness duration. This pattern—concurrent psychotic and mood (manic-predominant) symptoms, with psychotic symptoms extending beyond mood episodes, and mood symptoms present for the majority of the illness—is most consistent with Schizoaffective Disorder, Bipolar Type (F25.0), rather than primary Bipolar Disorder with psychotic features (which would require psychotic symptoms confined only to mood episodes) or Schizophrenia (which would require mood symptoms to be brief/absent relative to psychotic illness duration).
